title: Kansas police chief used Flock license plate cameras 164 times to track ex-girlfriend

reading.body:
This is a case of authorised access turned to a personal purpose. The system was a network of license plate readers, and the person using it held the credentials that made its use legitimate in ordinary police work. Nothing in the reporting suggests the technology malfunctioned or produced a wrong answer. The failure sits with the operator, not the model, and it is the kind of misuse that a system built for law enforcement queries is not designed to prevent on its own.

Catching it would have required looking at the queries rather than the results. A plate reader returns a location for a plate, and a search for a plate connected to a person the operator knows looks the same at the point of use as any other search. What distinguishes it is the pattern over time and the absence of a case reason attached to it, which means detection depends on query-level audit and someone reviewing who searched for whom. The reporting does not say whether any such review existed.

The count is not settled. The headline gives 164 uses and the summary gives 228, so the exact number of queries is not established here. The account comes from a certification order, and the conduct described in it is reported rather than adjudicated as a criminal finding.

reports.title: Kansas police chief used Flock license plate cameras 164 times to track ex-girlfriend

summary: From June to October 2023, Sedgwick, Kansas, Police Chief Lee Nygaard reportedly used Flock Safety license-plate readers 228 times to check where his ex-girlfriend and her new boyfriend were, according to a Kansas certification order. The order said he also followed them in a police vehicle and admitted jealousy influenced his conduct. Nygaard resigned in October 2023 and later lost his police certification.
title_en: Kansas police chief used Flock license plate cameras 164 times to track ex-girlfriend
